extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and the methodology of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for what counts as a cause and how to judge competing causal theories in philosophical and scientific discussion of causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as set of antecedents connected by invariable and unconditional sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: "That set, or those sets, of antecedents are its cause." — the cause of a phenomenon is the assemblage of antecedent conditions which are connected to the phenomenon by invariable and unconditional sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a proposed cause by identifying the specific antecedent conditions and asking whether those antecedents are invariably and unconditionally followed by the phenomenon. The text emphasizes treating the cause as the whole assemblage of antecedents rather than a single factor in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish force and collocation within the cause
rubrics_metrics.description: In the assemblage of conditions constituting the Cause distinguish two elements: one, the presence of a force; the other, the collocation or position of objects required for the force's particular transmutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing causal situations, explicitly separate (a) the active, changing element (force) and (b) the spatial/positional conditions (collocation) that permit the force to produce the observed effect. Examples given: bonfire (chemical action + collocated fuel/air/spark); grinding corn (collocation of mill parts + water gravitation or wind motion supplying force).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation: change can only be produced by change
rubrics_metrics.description: "The law of causation is, that change can only be produced by change." — at least one changing antecedent (a force) must be present among antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject accounts of causation that rely solely on stationary antecedents; ensure analyses identify what active change (force) is doing causal work. Use presence/absence of an active antecedent as a basic test for causal adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent may be potential, not actual, motion (potentiality of motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true definition of Force is not actual motion, but Potentiality of Motion; antecedent motion need not be actually taking place—for example, the stored 'force' in coal or the potential motion of a stone on an eminence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow that causal antecedents can be dispositional or potential properties rather than presently manifest motions. Analyses should treat stored or potential capacities to produce motion as legitimate antecedent elements of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as collocation of objects possessing the property (property-as-antecedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The force said to be stored up, is simply a particular property which the object has acquired... The cause we are in search of, is a collocation of objects possessing that particular property."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying causes, consider not only overt actions but properties objects possess that make them fit antecedents under particular collocations. The 'stored' force is a convenient linguistic device for such properties; treat them as non-mysterious dispositional antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditure or transfer of energy as a test distinguishing causation from mere concomitance
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted from Mr. Bain: one of the tests for distinguishing causation from mere concomitance is the expenditure or transfer of energy — if the effect consists in putting matter in motion, any object that has lost motion has contributed to the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measurable transfer or loss of energy/motion as evidence of causal contribution when the effect involves motion. This is offered as a practical test: identify whether any antecedent has undergone an energy decrement corresponding to the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require external empirical evidence, not subjective conceivability, for causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Volitional theory: subjective 'consciousness of effort' or feelings of power are not positive evidence that volition is an efficient cause independently of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject appeals to inward feeling or a priori conceivability as sufficient grounds for asserting causal powers. Insist on observable, empirical, or experiential evidence for claims that a particular kind of antecedent (e.g., volition) is an efficient cause of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from a single instance without resemblance of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When generalizing from one known instance to many, the instances must resemble the known case; one must not infer a universal from a single dissimilar instance (e.g., inferring all heavenly bodies are inhabited from only one inhabited world).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether candidate generalizations rest on adequate similarity in manifestations and laws; require comparable observable indicators before extending causal explanations from one case to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of familiarity bias in judging conceivability and causal plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: What persons can or cannot conceive is largely determined by their experience and habits of thought; familiarity makes some causal sequences seem natural and others inconceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust critical evaluation to account for cognitive bias: treat claims grounded primarily on what seems 'natural' or 'conceivable' with suspicion, and demand evidence that is independent of mere familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invoking supernatural or ad hoc agents when natural explanations suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Occasional Causes and invoking divine will: do not posit God or occult agents as a default efficient cause for physical phenomena simply because some connections seem inconceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural, testable explanations to metaphysical ad hoc hypotheses; require positive reason or evidence before substituting supernatural agency for mechanisms that can be empirically investigated.
